recap_title: 🐍 Comprehensive Python Basics Recap for Young Coders!
recap_subtitle: Hey, outstanding programmers! Let's take a look at the magical concepts and exciting scripts we created in our Python journey at Megaminds Academy. The sessions are grouped below:

points.title: What is Python?
points.desc: An incredibly popular, clean, high-level, and simple programming language that reads like plain English. It is heavily used in web building, data science, and Artificial Intelligence.
points.example: A clean, high-level language. Example: print("Hello, Python!")

points.title: Printing via print()
points.desc: The built-in function print() is our main channel to send messages from Python code, printing values, strings, or math outputs straight to the output screen.
points.code:
print("Welcome to Megaminds Academy! 🚀")
print(5 + 10)  # Prints 15

points.title: Variables as Data Boxes
points.desc: Variables are named, virtual boxes inside the computer memory used to store various data values (like text strings or integers) so we can reuse them later in our scripts.
points.code:
player_name = "Tobi"
score = 10
print(player_name)
print(score)

points.title: Python Data Types
points.desc: Different kinds of data do different things! Core types include text strings (str), numbers (int, float), sequences (list, tuple), mappings (dict), and true/false states (bool).
points.code:
name = "Alice"       # String (str)
age = 14             # Integer (int)
height = 1.65        # Float (float)
is_winner = True     # Boolean (bool)

points.title: User Inputs via input()
points.desc: The input() function pauses the program and allows visitors to type text. Note: input() always returns text as a string (str), so we convert it to numbers using int() or float() for math.
points.code:
# Always returns a string:
user_choice = input("Enter your choice: ")
# Convert to numbers for math:
age = int(input("Enter your age: "))

points.title: Python Lists & Indexes
points.desc: Lists store multiple items in a single variable using square brackets []. Elements are ordered, changeable, and zero-indexed (the first item is at index 0, the second at 1, etc.).
points.code:
colors = ["red", "green", "blue"]
print(colors[0])  # prints "red"
colors.append("yellow") # Adds item to end

points.title: Math Operators
points.desc: Python makes calculations easy! We use standard symbols: + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), and / (division) to compute complex mathematical values.

points.title: Comparison & Assignment Operators
points.desc: Assignment operators like = and += store values. Comparison operators like == (equals), != (not equals), >, and < check values, returning a True or False Boolean.
points.code:
x = 10
x += 5   # x is now 15
is_greater = (x > 12)  # True

points.title: String Indexing
points.desc: A string acts like an unchangeable list of characters! We can extract individual characters using brackets, where the space character also counts as an index position.
points.code:
msg = "Python"
print(msg[0])  # Prints 'P'
print(msg[-1]) # Prints 'n' (last char)

points.title: Ordered & Immutable Tuples
points.desc: Tuples store multiple items in a single variable using round brackets (). Unlike lists, tuples are immutable, meaning their elements cannot be changed or edited after creation.
points.code:
coordinates = (10, 20)  # Cannot be changed!
# coordinates[0] = 15 -> Error!

points.title: Dictionaries as Key-Value Pairs
points.desc: Dictionaries store data in structured key:value pairs using curly brackets {}. They do not allow duplicate keys and let you retrieve values instantly using their unique keys.

points.title: Comparing Python Data Structures
points.desc: We use lists [] when items change, tuples () when items must stay constant for safety, and dictionaries {} when linking identifiers to specific descriptions.
points.code:
my_list = [1, 2]     # list [] (changeable)
my_tuple = (1, 2)    # tuple () (unchangeable)
my_dict = {"a": 1}   # dict {} (key:value)

points.title: Smart Decision Making (if-elif-else)
points.desc: If-statements check conditions to run specific blocks of code. We use 'elif' to check additional conditions, and 'else' as a fallback when all other tests fail.

points.title: Conditional Loop (while)
points.desc: A while loop runs a block of code repeatedly as long as its condition remains True. We must increment our loop variable to avoid building a dangerous infinite loop!
points.code:
count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print("Count:", count)
    count += 1

points.title: Loop Controls: break & continue
points.desc: Use the 'break' statement to exit a loop immediately, and 'continue' to skip the remaining code in the current round and jump straight to the next loop cycle.

sessions.session_title: 🔄 Session 6: For Loops, Range & Nested Loops

points.title: For Loops & Sequences
points.desc: A for-loop is used to iterate over sequence collections (lists, tuples, dicts) or characters in a string, performing an action for every element in order.

points.title: The range() Function
points.desc: Generates a sequence of numbers starting from 0 by default, incrementing by 1, and stopping before a specified number (e.g. range(5) yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4).

points.title: Nested Loops
points.desc: A loop inside another loop! The inner loop completes all its cycles once for every single iteration of the outer loop, which is useful for grid coordinates.

points.title: Writing Functions (def)
points.desc: A function is a reusable block of code created using the def keyword. It only executes when explicitly called by its name followed by parentheses.
points.code:
def greet_user(name):
    return "Hello, " + name + "! 🌟"

# Call it:
msg = greet_user("Alice")
print(msg)

points.title: Parameters vs. Arguments
points.desc: Parameters are the variables defined in a function's parenthesis. Arguments are the actual, real values passed into the function when we call it.
points.code:
def show_age(name, age): # name, age are parameters
    print(name, "is", age)

show_age("Tobi", 12)     # "Tobi", 12 are arguments

points.title: Returning Values
points.desc: Functions perform work and can send results back to the caller using the 'return' statement, which also stops the function's execution immediately.
points.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(10, 5)
print(result) # 15

points.title: Importing External Libraries
points.desc: Libraries are pre-written modules that handle complex tasks so we don't write them from scratch. We search packages on PyPI and install them using pip.
points.code:
import random
num = random.randint(1, 10)
print("Random:", num)

points.title: Turtle Drawing Canvas
points.desc: The built-in Turtle module allows us to control a virtual pen (turtle) on a graphic canvas to draw custom shapes, lines, and colorful geometric designs.
points.code:
import turtle
t = turtle.Turtle()
t.forward(100)
t.left(90)
turtle.done()

points.title: Turtle Customizers
points.desc: We can change pen colors, adjust pen sizes, set fill colors, and control turtle speeds using simple built-in methods like color(), pensize(), and speed().
points.code:
t.color("blue")
t.pensize(5)
t.speed(10)
t.begin_fill()
t.circle(50)
t.end_fill()

points.title: Classes vs. Objects
points.desc: A Class is a blueprint or template (like a blueprint for a Car). An Object is an actual instance created from that blueprint (like a specific red Tesla).

points.title: The __init__ Constructor
points.desc: A special, built-in initializer function that runs automatically whenever we create a new object, setting up its starting properties and variables.

points.title: Understanding the self Parameter
points.desc: The 'self' keyword points directly to the active object we are creating or modifying, letting us access and update its properties from within the class.

points.title: The requests Library
points.desc: A powerful Python library used to interact with web servers by sending HTTP requests (like GET and POST) to fetch web pages or submit forms.
points.code:
import requests
response = requests.get("https://api.github.com")
print(response.status_code) # 200

points.title: Brute Force & Hacking Scrips
points.desc: A security concept where scripts systematically try dictionary combinations to crack weak passwords or test security robustness on local targets.

points.title: Web Servers with Flask
points.desc: Flask is a micro web framework in Python that allows us to set up routes, receive browser connections, and run our own local web servers easily.

sessions.session_title: 🎮 Session 11: Ping Pong Game - Object Initialization

points.title: Setting Up the Game Canvas
points.desc: Using the Turtle library to open a custom graphics window, configure its width and height, set a dark theme background, and turn off auto-tracer updates.
points.code:
import turtle
win = turtle.Screen()
win.title("Ping Pong Game")
win.bgcolor("black")
win.setup(width=800, height=600)
win.tracer(0) # turn off auto updates

points.title: Creating Paddles & Ball
points.desc: Initializing turtle objects representing player paddles and a game ball. We customize their shapes to squares/circles and position them on the canvas.
points.code:
paddle = turtle.Turtle()
paddle.speed(0)
paddle.shape("square")
paddle.color("white")
paddle.shapesize(stretch_wid=5, stretch_len=1)
paddle.penup()
paddle.goto(-350, 0)

points.title: Visual Center Markers
points.desc: Drawing dotted or solid lines down the center of our screen and setting up scoreboards using turtle.write() to show player scores in real-time.
points.code:
pen = turtle.Turtle()
pen.speed(0)
pen.color("white")
pen.penup()
pen.hideturtle()
pen.goto(0, 260)
pen.write("Player A: 0  Player B: 0", align="center", font=("Courier", 24, "normal"))

sessions.session_title: 🕹️ Session 12: Ping Pong Game - Input Controls & Physics

points.title: Key Bindings & Event Listening
points.desc: Connecting paddle movement functions to specific keyboard keys (like 'W' and 'S' or Arrow Keys) using turtle.onkeypress() and turtle.listen().
points.code:
def paddle_up():
    y = paddle.ycor()
    paddle.sety(y + 20)

win.listen()
win.onkeypress(paddle_up, "w") # calls paddle_up when W is pressed

points.title: Ball Physics & Collision Rules
points.desc: Updating ball positions in a while-loop. We detect border collisions to bounce the ball, and paddle coordinates to reverse the ball's horizontal velocity.
points.code:
# Inside game loop:
ball.setx(ball.xcor() + ball.dx)
ball.sety(ball.ycor() + ball.dy)

# Border collision:
if ball.ycor() > 290:
    ball.sety(290)
    ball.dy *= -1 # reverse direction

points.title: Scores & Resetting Play
points.desc: When the ball passes a paddle, we credit a point to the opposing player, reset the ball to the center, and update the scoreboard dynamically.
points.code:
# If ball goes past left paddle:
if ball.xcor() < -390:
    ball.goto(0, 0)
    ball.dx *= -1
    score_b += 1
    update_scoreboard()
